subject: Re: [r-inla] Consider measurement errors in the spatial model

messages.author: 3eab71733027a24a
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Consider measurement errors in the spatial model
parts:
Hi & thanks for your email. Its a lot here...


On Sat, 2016-10-22 at 15:37 -0700, Xiaojun Pu wrote:
> I have a spatial model for disease mapping, which is a revision of
> the spatial moving average model.
>
> y ~ b1*x1 + (I + rho*W)*b2*x2 + e, 
>
> e ~ N(0, sigma^2*(I+rho*W)*t(I+rho*W)).              Note: t(I+rho*W)
> is the transpose of (I+rho*W)
>
> y is cancer mortality rate.  x1 and x2 are different covariates. W is
> a covariance matrix, which is not the common spatial adjacency matrix
> with only 0 and 1.
>
> I have revised the slm.inla() in INLABMA package to get this
> function. The INLA formula of this model is:
>
> IrhoW <- solve(diag(nrow(W)) + rho * W)
> IrhoW2 <- t(IrhoW) %*% IrhoW
>
> y ~ x1 + (I + rho*W)*x2 + f(idx, model = "generic0", Cmatrix =
> IrhoW2), 

I cannot see that this formula will do what you want. There is no pre-
made model now that can do this. You can use the new tool, rgeneric,
see inla.doc("rgeneric")  to define this model, including the mean (I +
rho*W)*b2*x2. the parmeter b2 can either be a hyperparameter, which is
easier, or in the latent field, a bit more complex.   see the
documentation and let me know if you run into problems.

> (1) In each spatial unit, the cancer mortality rate y has an estimate
> (y_mean) and a margin of error (y_e = 1.65*se). The dependent
> variable y in the model is actually the estimate y_mean. I read some
> documents said using control.family() to set the precision of y. And
> some documents said use f(idx, y_mean, model="iid") to include the
> uncertainty. Could anyone tell me what is the difference between
> these two methods?
> The margin of errors for different spatial units are different. And I
> don't know whether they come from the same distribution. Usually, the
> spatial unit with a large population should have a small error and
> vice versa. Is that possible to catch up the various uncertainty of
> cancer mortality rate for each spatial unit by using one vector y_e?

the normal way to define the likelihood in an observation is to use
family="gaussian", say and you can control the precision using
control.family and argument 'hyper'. in some, difficult cases, there is
a need to 'move' the likelihood into the model, like you write above,
where there is no 'iid' noise, just the error 'e' which is correlated.
do you fake this adding 'e' into the linear predictor, and then setting
the Gaussian noise to essentially zero, like a high precision which is
fixed. 

> (2) W is a covariance matrix which is not deterministic because the
> values are count estimates. Suppose W is a 10*10 matrix, so I have a
> total of 100 cells. For each cell, I have both estimate (W_mean) and
> the corresponding margin of error (W_e). Now I can have two 10*10
> matrices: W_mean and W_e. In the spatial model, the estimate matrix
> W_mean is regarded as the covariance matrix W. Is that possible to
> include the error matrix W_e in the model to adjust the uncertainty
> of W_mean?

you can emulate this using the Wishart distrubtion, and then sample
from this and run inla() M times, say, and then you get the uncertainty
wrt W. you cannot do this in one inla()-call. 



hope this helps.
